thread.title: Are The Monthly Charts Warning About Apple's Earnings?

author: Tom Aspray
title: Are The Monthly Charts Warning About Apple's Earnings?
text:
The S&P 500 dropped 0.67% on Monday, in the largest decline since last September. Part of the decline was the 2.1% drop in the stock of Apple, Inc. (AAPL), which was a drag on all of the major averages, as well as the technology sector. The largest holding in the Technology Select Sector (XLK) is Apple, with a portfolio weight of 13.74%.
The Apple Store in Pittsburgh (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)
The stock market declined even more sharply on Tuesday with the Dow Industrials and S&P 500 dropping more than 1%. Apple was down another 0.52% to close at $167.05.
Investors are now even more focused on the earnings for Apple, which are scheduled to be released after the close on February 1 st . Many other tech giants, including Microsoft Inc. (MSFT) and Facebook (FB), are also reporting this week, but Apple has garnered most of the interest.
Often times, signs of a disappointing earnings report will be evident in the charts, as they were last June for Micron Technology (MU). As a long-term market technician, I have always felt it was important to look at the monthly charts in order to assess a stock’s trend ahead of an earnings report.
Tom Aspray - ViperReport.com
With the decline on Monday, Apple stock is now trading below $168.43 where it closed last October. The stock did make a new all-time high at $180.10 earlier this month. A doji was formed in December. A doji forms when the opening and closing price are almost the same.
In December 2017, Apple opened the month at $169.95 and closed at $169.23. The doji formation is often a sign of indecision. When a stock or ETF closes below the doji low, that triggers a doji sell signal. This normally occurs within three periods after the doji. On the chart, I have highlighted the doji sell signals that occurred in October 2012 and in July of 2015.
In both instances, Apple declined for many months before it again turned higher. A January close below $166.46 will trigger a monthly doji sell signal. If this does not occur in January, investors should still look out for a doji sell signal in February or March. For more information on doji formations, see my “Candle Magic” article from June.
The relative performance (RS) measures how a stock is performing relative to the S&P 500 or Spyder Trust (SPY). When the RS is above its own Weighted Moving Average (WMA), it means Apple is performing stronger than the market averages.
Since the start of 2017, this has been the case, but it now looks very likely that the RS will drop below its WMA at the end of January. This would mean that Apple is going to underperform the S&P 500.
The on-balance-volume (OBV) is another of my favorite technical tools. Increases in the OBV are often an indicator of increased demand. When prices are moving higher, but the OBV is not, then a divergence is formed.
These negative or bearish divergences can alert the investor or trader to a potential peak in prices. The monthly OBV for Apple peaked in May 2015. Even though the stock is now about 30% higher than it was in 2015, the OBV has formed lower highs (line a). The OBV is likely to finish the month above its WMA but it will bear watching as we head into February.
It is also important to note that Apple is trading just above its quarterly pivot at $166.30. This level is calculated from the prior quarter’s high, low and closing price. A Friday close below the quarterly pivot often signals a downward trend in prices, as I discussed in a past Forbes post, “Investors Should Follow The Quarterly Trend.”
There are also some other support and resistance levels to watch in the next few weeks. In addition to the quarterly pivot, there is additional support now in the $161.20 area. Even if Apple completes a monthly top, an upward rebound is still likely in the next several weeks. The first resistance level to watch is at $170-$171 with stronger in the $173-$174 area.
